title: Camera control through ONVIF
description: Understand the Agent connection behind remote camera controls and why support depends on the camera.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional warehouse operator who wants to turn a camera while watching it in Hub. Does the browser connect directly to every camera's private control interface?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The guide describes a different route. The Agent is connected to its camera through ONVIF, and Hub forwards supported control actions to the Agent over the bidirectional messaging connection. That connection lets the Agent handle the camera-side work.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So we need more than a camera-shaped icon on the live page?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. ONVIF must be enabled and configured on the Agent, the camera must support the relevant capabilities, and the messaging connection needs to work. Camera support varies, including the ONVIF profiles it implements.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What does pan, tilt and zoom mean for the operator's everyday task?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It's the family of controls used to direct a supported camera. This guide illustrates directional movement and returning to the centre from the live view. It also distinguishes available controls from features described as future work, so don't assume every control exists on every device.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: A remote control, not a promise that a fixed camera will grow motors. What's our next step?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Check the camera's supported features, confirm the Agent's ONVIF setup and connection, and try a supported action in live view. Use the linked guide for the connection picture and the current live-view documentation for the controls available in your deployment.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
